subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxide is added to fields by farmers. What is its main agricultural use?
options: To neutralise acidic soils (raise the pH)
questions.explain: Ca(OH)2 is a base used to neutralise acidic soils, raising their pH.

questions.q: Why is a small amount of chlorine added to drinking water despite its toxicity?
options: To increase the pH of the water
Its benefit in killing harmful microorganisms outweighs the risk of toxic effects
questions.explain: Chlorine kills pathogenic bacteria, so the public-health benefit is judged to outweigh the toxic risks.

questions.q: How does the reactivity of Group 2 metals change down the group, and why?
options: Increases, because ionisation energies decrease as outer electrons get further from the nucleus
questions.explain: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are lost more easily (lower ionisation energies) because they are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so reactivity increases.

questions.q: Why does the [Al(H2O)6]3+ ion act as a weak acid in water?
options: The high charge density polarises coordinated water, weakening O-H bonds so H+ is released
questions.explain: The 3+ charge on the small Al3+ ion withdraws electron density from O-H bonds of ligand water, releasing H+ and lowering the pH.

questions.q: The Contact process uses V2O5 as a catalyst; this is an example of:
options: Homogeneous catalysis using variable oxidation states (V being reduced to V2O4 then re-oxidised)
questions.explain: V2O5 oxidises SO2 and is reduced to V2O4, then re-oxidised by O2, cycling between +5 and +4 oxidation states.

questions.q: How does the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates change down the group?
options: Solubility decreases down the group, with BaSO4 essentially insoluble
questions.explain: Group 2 sulfate solubility decreases down the group; BaSO4 is essentially insoluble, which is why barium sulfate is used in the test for sulfate ions.

questions.q: Which observation correctly identifies the result of adding silver nitrate to a solution containing iodide ions?
options: White precipitate, soluble in dilute ammonia
Cream precipitate, soluble in concentrated ammonia
Yellow precipitate, insoluble in concentrated ammonia
questions.explain: Iodide gives a yellow AgI precipitate that does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia.

questions.q: Why is barium more reactive than calcium toward water?
options: Calcium has a larger atomic radius than barium
Barium has a higher first ionisation energy so reacts faster
Barium has fewer protons than calcium
Barium's outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily, making it more reactive
questions.explain: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are further out and more shielded, lowering ionisation energy, so barium loses electrons (and reacts) more readily than calcium.

questions.q: What type of ligand is the ethanedioate (oxalate) ion, C2O4 2-?
questions.explain: Ethanedioate donates two lone pairs from two oxygen atoms, making it a bidentate ligand.

questions.q: What is meant by autocatalysis in the reaction between manganate(VII) and ethanedioate?
options: A product, Mn2+, catalyses the reaction so the rate increases as it proceeds
questions.explain: Mn2+ is a product that catalyses the reaction, so the rate increases once some Mn2+ has formed.

questions.q: Which factor would change the colour (wavelength absorbed) of a transition-metal complex?
options: Changing the volume of solvent only
questions.explain: Different ligands cause different d-orbital splitting energies, altering the wavelength absorbed and hence the observed colour.

questions.q: What is the coordination number and shape of a complex ion with six monodentate ligands such as [Fe(H2O)6]2+?
questions.explain: Six monodentate ligands each donate one lone pair, giving coordination number 6 and an octahedral shape.

questions.q: In the reaction MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ -> Mn2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe3+, the oxidation state of manganese changes from:
questions.explain: Manganese is reduced from +7 in MnO4- to +2 in Mn2+, gaining five electrons.

questions.q: Why is acidified barium chloride solution used to test for sulfate ions, and why is magnesium hydroxide used in medicine?
options: BaSO4 is soluble; Mg(OH)2 is a strong acid
Both compounds are soluble and coloured
BaSO4 is green; Mg(OH)2 is a strong oxidiser
BaSO4 forms a white precipitate as it is insoluble; Mg(OH)2 is a sparingly soluble base used as an antacid
questions.explain: The insolubility of BaSO4 gives a white precipitate confirming sulfate, while sparingly soluble Mg(OH)2 neutralises stomach acid as 'milk of magnesia'.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium oxide, Na2O, is added to water?
options: It dissolves to give a strongly alkaline solution of NaOH
questions.explain: Na2O reacts vigorously with water to form sodium hydroxide, giving a solution of around pH 13-14.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide gives the most acidic solution when added to water?
questions.explain: SO3 reacts with water to form sulfuric acid, a strong acid, giving the lowest pH of the Period 3 oxides.

questions.q: Why is MgO only slightly soluble and weakly alkaline in water compared with Na2O?
options: Mg2+ has a higher charge density and MgO has stronger ionic bonding, limiting its reaction with water
MgO does not contain oxide ions
questions.explain: The stronger lattice and higher charge density of Mg2+ make MgO sparingly soluble, giving only a weakly alkaline suspension (about pH 9-10).

questions.q: What colour change is seen when concentrated HCl is added to aqueous [Cu(H2O)6]2+?
questions.explain: Chloride ligands substitute the water ligands forming the yellow tetrahedral [CuCl4]2-, giving a green mixture with the blue aqua ion.

questions.q: Which definition best describes a transition metal?
options: A d-block metal that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d-subshell
A metal with a full d-subshell
A metal that forms only +2 ions
questions.explain: Sc and Zn are excluded because their stable ions (Sc3+, Zn2+) have empty or full d-subshells, respectively.

questions.q: How does the solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides change down the group?
options: All Group 2 hydroxides are equally insoluble
Solubility is greatest for magnesium hydroxide
questions.explain: Group 2 hydroxide solubility increases down the group, so Mg(OH)2 is least soluble and Ba(OH)2 most soluble.

questions.q: Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate in the test for halide ions?
options: To increase the solubility of the silver halides
To reduce the silver ions to silver
To remove carbonate or hydroxide ions that would otherwise give a false precipitate
questions.explain: Acidifying with nitric acid removes interfering ions such as carbonate and hydroxide that would form precipitates with silver nitrate.

questions.q: Which Group 2 metal reacts most vigorously with water?
questions.explain: Reactivity with water increases down Group 2, so barium reacts most vigorously of these.

questions.q: Why are most aqueous transition-metal ions coloured?
options: s-electrons are excited to higher p-orbitals
Electrons are promoted between split d-orbitals, absorbing certain wavelengths of visible light
The metals emit light by nuclear decay
questions.explain: Ligands split the d-orbitals; absorption of visible light promotes a d-electron, and the complementary colour is transmitted.

questions.q: Why is dilute sulfuric acid, rather than HCl, used to acidify manganate(VII) titrations?
options: Chloride ions would be oxidised by MnO4-, giving a false result
questions.explain: MnO4- would oxidise Cl- to Cl2, consuming extra MnO4- and over-reading the titre, so non-oxidisable H2SO4 is used.

questions.q: In the reaction Cl2 + H2O gives HCl + HClO, what are the oxidation states of chlorine in the products?
questions.explain: Chlorine is reduced to -1 in HCl and oxidised to +1 in HClO, a disproportionation of chlorine (0) used in water treatment.

questions.q: What happens when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?
options: A white precipitate of KCl forms
The solution turns orange as chlorine displaces bromine
questions.explain: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it displaces bromine: Cl2 + 2Br- gives 2Cl- + Br2, giving an orange colour.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point of the halogens increase down Group 7?
options: Metallic bonding develops down the group
Hydrogen bonding increases down the group
Covalent bonds within molecules get stronger
Molecules get larger with more electrons, so London (van der Waals) forces between molecules increase
questions.explain: Larger halogen molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.q: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy across Period 3, and the main reason?
options: It increases because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
It decreases because atomic radius increases
It stays constant because the shell is the same
questions.explain: First ionisation energy generally rises across Period 3 as increasing nuclear charge attracts the outer electrons more strongly with little change in shielding.

questions.q: Which species is responsible for the deep blue colour formed when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?
questions.explain: Ammonia partially substitutes water to give the deep blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ ion.

questions.q: Silicon dioxide, SiO2, when classified by its acid-base behaviour is best described as:
options: An acidic oxide that is insoluble in water but reacts with hot concentrated alkali
An amphoteric oxide that dissolves in acid
questions.explain: SiO2 is acidic, reacting with hot concentrated NaOH to form a silicate, though it is insoluble in water.
